picked.title: Isaac Lab v3.0.0
picked.summary: Isaac Lab 3.0 Isaac Lab 3.0 is now generally available. v3.0.0 is the official Isaac Lab 3.0 release and the recommended baseline for new projects and migrations from Isaac Lab 2.x. Isaac Lab 3.0 establishes the foundation for the next generation of robot learning in Isaac Lab: one task API across multiple physics, rendering, and visualization backends; kit-less execution with Newton and OV library backends; Warp-native data paths; and unified workflows from installation through training, evaluation, and deployment. Newton is a Warp-native physics backend with multiple solver paths, including MuJoCo-Warp, VBD, and MPM. It lets Isaac Lab support rigid bodies, deformables, and particles without tying tasks to one physics engine. OV Libraries provide OVPhysX for PhysX and OVRTX for RTX rendering as standalone libraries. Isaac Sim remains the complete path when a workflow needs the full PhysX/RTX stack, ROS bridge, XR, livestreaming, or Kit tooling, but now fully optional. MicroDuck rendering VBD cable insertion MPM liquid pouring One task API; install and run only the capabilities you need. This release targets Isaac Sim 6.2, Python 3.12, PyTorch 2.11 with CUDA 13.0, NVIDIA Warp 1.17, Newton 1.6.1, and RSL-RL 5.5.1. Try Isaac Lab 3.0 Install uv , clone the official release, and launch a Newton workflow: git clone --branch v3.0.0 --depth 1 https://github.com/isaac-sim/IsaacLab.git cd IsaacLab uv run isaaclab train \ --rl_library rsl_rl \ --task Isaac-Cartpole \ --viz newton_gl \ physics=newton_mjwarp For standalone PhysX and RTX rendering, install the OV libraries: uv run --extra ov isaaclab train \ --rl_library rsl_rl \ --task Isaac-Cartpole-Camera \ --viz newton_gl \ physics=ovphysx \ renderer=ovrtx \ presets=rgb For the complete Isaac Sim experience, including Isaac Sim PhysX, Isaac Sim RTX, ROS bridge, XR, livestreaming, and Kit tooling: uv run --extra isaacsim isaaclab train \ --rl_library rsl_rl \ --task Isaac-Cartpole \ --viz kit \ physics=isaacsim_physx See the …

picked.title: Know When to Escalate: Critic-Guided Adaptive Execution for Cloud-Local Embodied Agents
picked.summary: Recent advances in foundation-model agents have enabled increasingly capable embodied systems for long-horizon planning and interaction. However, embodied agents require fast, closed-loop decisions as they continuously perceive and act on a changing environment. Deploying strong cloud agents leaves the platform idle for seconds between consecutive actions, while lightweight local models respond quickly but are more vulnerable to errors. Existing hierarchical architectures typically assign models fixed roles, whereas conventional model routers make stateless per-request decisions. We present CARE, a critic-guided adaptive execution framework that dynamically determines when to escalate control from a local executor to a stronger cloud model. A lightweight critic model monitors execution reliability and triggers escalation when local execution becomes unreliable; once escalated, control persists until the agent recovers, avoiding step-wise switching. To support such control transfer, a shared handoff memory maintains execution context and task-level progress across executors, enabling the model to intervene without restarting from scratch. Across diverse embodied benchmarks, CARE improves task success by 6.3-18.3 percentage points over the strongest evaluated collaboration baseline. CARE further approaches or exceeds Cloud-only success while reducing median time-between-action latency by 28.8-82.6%.

picked.title: TEAR: Task-Evidence Authority Routing for Robotic Manipulation
picked.summary: Reliable robotic manipulation in field-deployed settings requires more than executing a capable controller. As the execution conditions change, the system must decide, online and on the robot side, which control source should hold authority. Human teleoperation adapts readily to contact-rich and semantically ambiguous situations but depends on a stable communication link. Local autonomy is executed without continuous human intervention, but may fail under semantic ambiguity, long-horizon drift, and unforeseen contingencies. These two control sources exhibit complementary reliability profiles. We formulate this complementarity as a control authority routing problem and present Task-Evidence Authority Routing for Robotic Manipulation (TEAR), an edge-deployable framework that allocates authority between human teleoperation and local autonomy. TEAR arbitrates on the robot side using network-state evidence, which governs the usability of teleoperation, and task-semantic evidence, which reflects whether autonomous execution remains consistent with the current task. A lightweight temporal arbitrator observes both forms of evidence together with robot state and current authority to time authority transfers. Across simulated and real-world trials under dynamic network conditions, TEAR achieves task success rates close to pure teleoperation while limiting teleoperation to 19.8-27.4% of control steps and improves success by 30-40% over autonomy-only execution in our settings. These results demonstrate the potential of complementary authority routing to sustain successful manipulation with substantially reduced dependence on continuous human control.

picked.title: Learning Robot Behavior Priors from Non-Robotic Synthetic Data
picked.summary: Real robot data, rich across tasks and morphologies, is often treated as the bottleneck for training robot learning models, including embodied foundation models that aim for zero-shot physical transfer. In this paper, we investigate the degree to which such models can acquire necessary structure using data from systems without embodiment. To this end, we test if inexpensive, procedurally generated synthetic data can yield useful priors before a model observes any real-world behavior. We study this through robot action prediction, a natural pretraining objective and a direct test of whether structure learned from arbitrary synthetic tasks transfers to embodied settings. We introduce three data generation pipelines that model mathematical abstractions of robotic control, and use them as pretraining priors for a Transformer. We demonstrate that a model trained purely on this non-robotic data attains non-trivial zero-shot prediction performance on unseen physical robot tasks via an in-context learning mechanism, and that our specialized control priors notably improve upon generic causal priors. We also compare against a compute-matched baseline trained on real robot data, and find that it outperforms our model but only on the datasets it was trained on. These findings suggest that procedurally generated, mathematical abstractions can yield useful robotic priors, offering a potential complement to expensive embodied data collection.

picked.title: Point-Level Refinable Semantic Mapping for Spatial Understanding
picked.summary: Open-vocabulary 3D semantic maps have emerged as a key spatial memory representation for long-horizon robot autonomy, enabling robots to reason about objects, their spatial relationships, and past observations across time. However, existing object-centric semantic maps are primarily designed for static environments and rely on an append-only point integration strategy, where newly observed points are accumulated but previously integrated points are rarely reevaluated. Consequently, perception errors accumulate over time, and outdated points persist after objects move or disappear. Although recent dynamic mapping methods update object-level representations in changing scenes, they do not explicitly revise noisy or obsolete points within each object. We propose an online refinable semantic mapping framework that continuously refines object representations through probabilistic point-level confidence updating. Each object point maintains a confidence score that is updated online using multi-view temporal evidence: consistent observations reinforce reliable points, while inconsistent segmentation masks, depth measurements, and visibility cues suppress spurious and outdated points. Combined with object tracking and re-identification to preserve instance identities under motion and relocation, our framework enables object-centric semantic maps to be continuously refined rather than monotonically accumulated. Experiments demonstrate improved mapping accuracy over the previous method by 3.46% on Replica and 2.55% on ScanNet, show robustness in dynamic environments and under perception noise, and provide an effective spatial memory for object navigation and embodied question-answering with success rates of 82.4% and 76.7%.
